newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia wants Pol Pot captured alive for trial.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia wants Pol Pot captured alive for trial.

text.p: Cambodia said on Tuesday it wanted to capture fugitive Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pot to stand trial before a world tribunal as former comrades turned enemies were said to be pursuing him deeper into the jungle.
"I hope that we will be able to take Pol Pot alive and send him to an international court," First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh told reporters in Phnom Penh.

Pol Pot, mastermind of the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge "killing fields" rule of Cambodia, was reported to be on the run toward Thailand with a handful of followers, holding several senior guerrillas, including front man Khieu Samphan, as hostages.

His flight looked to be the fatal blow to the reviled Maoist faction, hit by thousands of defections over the past 10 months and now apparently split irreparably over whether to make peace with Phnom Penh. Former comrades who had now defected to the government were hot on the trail of the leader, who fled his stronghold of Anlong Veng after slaughtering his defence chief and 11 of his family members, according to officials in Phnom Penh.
The guerrillas' clandestine radio station appeared to confirm the reports on Tuesday when it broke a four-day silence and broadcast a statement accusing Pol Pot of betraying his comrades.

"From the ninth to 14th of June, there were betrayals by Pol Pot. But this problem has been solved quietly by the unity forces," said an announcement read during broadcasts on Monday evening and Tuesday morning.
Thailand and Cambodia have sealed their border in the area to prevent him from escaping.
Thai army chief General Chetta Tanajaro said in Bangkok that Pol Pot was still hiding in Cambodia and would be arrested if he crossed into Thailand.
"He (Pol Pot) will not escape to Thailand. I can reassure you that because he knows once he enters the country the chance of being arrested and detained is high," he added.

Thomas Hammarberg, a senior U.N. human rights official, said on Tuesday that Cambodia's two prime ministers had said they would likely ask the United Nations to help convene an international tribunal to bring Pol Pot and others responsible for the "killing fields" to justice.

More than one million people died during the Khmer Rouge's reign from executions, starvation, disease and hard labour. "The important thing is that the international procedure start as soon as possible," Hammarberg told a news conference.
Khmer Rouge radio, which appeared to be in the hands of anti-Pol Pot guerrillas, said its statement was from a provisional government loyal to Khieu Samphan and his National Solidarity Party.
Khieu Samphan, who has been the president of the Khmer Rouge's provisional government for years, recently announced he wanted to form a political alliance with Cambodian co-premier Ranariddh.
About 95 percent of the rebels in Anlong Veng and a group of rebels with Pol Pot want to join the government, Ranariddh has said.
Khmer Rouge radio took the side of Ranariddh on Tuesday, expressing support for his political alliance but speaking out against his second premier Hun Sen.

Hun Sen was with the Vietnamese invasion force that eventually overthrew the Khmer Rouge regime and later led the Hanoi-backed government that ruled until 1991. He then formed an uneasy alliance with Ranariddh after U.N.-backed elections in 1993.

Hun Sen has criticised Ranariddh for holding talks with Khieu Samphan and said that negotiating with the guerrillas was illegal. Relations between the co-premiers have grown increasingly hostile as they manoeuvre ahead of expected elections next year.
On Tuesday, Ranariddh said he would draw the line only at co-operation with Pol Pot or his northern commander, Ta Mok.
"There are only two -- Ta Mok and Pol Pot -- who will not be given any amnesty," Ranariddh said. Ta Mok has broken with Pol Pot and disappeared, he said.
Not everyone is convinced that Ta Mok or other rebels have broken with Pol Pot, and many question Ranariddh's statements that Khieu Samphan is now a hostage of the rebel strongman.
Analysts said the story may have been cooked up to differentiate Khieu Samphan from the much-reviled Pol Pot to make him and his followers more palatable to the public.
